title: Ludwigia decurrens: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Ludwigia decurrens in Rice Fields: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Studies abroad link Ludwigia decurrens to a 33 percent rice yield loss. Learn to spot this winged stem kahoy kahoy weed and stop it early.
excerpt: Ludwigia decurrens is an upright, yellow flowered broadleaf weed that farmers call Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. It grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it by its winged stems, and how to control it before it sheds its seed.

heroImage.alt: Wingleaf primrose willow (Ludwigia decurrens), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: DouglasGoldman, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
In English, Ludwigia decurrens is called wingleaf primrose willow. It belongs to the evening primrose family, Onagraceae. In the bukid, farmers use the names Kahoy kahoy, malapako and tina tina. But these same names also cover its close relatives, so look at the stem to tell them apart. Being a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You can find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. As an annual, each plant finishes its life in one season. Seed is its only way to spread. The seeds form inside angled, narrowly winged pods, and they fall onto the soil when the pods open. Then they wait for the next cropping and sprout along with the palay.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Ludwigia decurrens
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Check the stem first. It stands upright, feels smooth, and has four thin wings running along its length. That winged stem is your best clue. The leaves sit almost flat on the stem, with hardly any stalk, and are narrow and pointed with smooth edges. Like other broadleaf weeds, its leaves have netted veins, unlike the parallel veins of grasses and sedges. The yellow flowers have four big petals with sharp tips, and the pods are sharply angled or narrowly winged.

items: Upright, smooth stems with four thin wings running down their whole length.
Narrow, lance shaped leaves sitting almost flat on the stem, with smooth edges.
Yellow flowers with four big petals that each end in a sharp tip.
Seed pods that are sharply angled or carry narrow wings, much like the stem.
Look alike tip: its kahoy kahoy cousins have angled or ridged stems, not winged ones.

blocks.text:
Here in the Philippines, there is no reported scientific proof yet that Ludwigia decurrens lowers rice yield. But studies in other countries found that it could cut rice yield by 33 percent when 4 to 8 plants grow in each square meter. So even a modest stand deserves your attention.

Other studies found that this weed is allelopathic to rice. That means it releases substances that can hold back the growth of rice plants nearby. Some variants have also become resistant to a certain herbicide. Because of this, do not count on a single product to clear it. Hand weeding and good water care still matter.

items: Pull plants by hand while they are young, before the yellow flowers turn into winged seed pods.
Since it spreads only by seed, never let a plant flower on the bunds or field edges, where seed can wash into the paddy.
Do not depend on one herbicide year after year, because some variants have already become resistant to a certain herbicide.
Bring pulled plants with flowers or pods out of the field, since pods left on the mud can still open and drop seed.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Ludwigia decurrens down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.title: When a spray stops working
blocks.text: Studies in other countries found that some variants of this weed have developed resistance to a certain herbicide, so rotate products and do not rely on one.

Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Ludwigia decurrens Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Ludwigia decurrens?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Ludwigia decurrens

items.q: What is Ludwigia decurrens called in Tagalog and other local names?
items.a: Farmers call it Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. In English it is the wingleaf primrose willow. Keep in mind that the same local names are used for other Ludwigia weeds too. To be sure you have this one, look for the four thin wings that run along the stem.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field, then keep shallow water where you can. Hand weed early and remove plants before they flower. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Since some variants resist a certain herbicide, switch products, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is this weed harmful to my palay?
items.a: It can be. Studies abroad found yield losses of 33 percent at 4 to 8 plants per square meter. The weed is also allelopathic, so it can hold back nearby rice. No such loss has been reported here in the Philippines yet. Still, each plant drops many seeds, so a few plants today can mean a thick stand next season.
